 Scrolling into Hallyu: How Korean webtoons are making their mark in Bangladesh 
 Because they were created for the digital age, webtoons fit particularly well into the way young Bangladeshis already consume culture – through a phone, a screen, and a constant stream of recommendations from friends and social media. 
 Samia Mahbub 
 31 October, 2026, 04:55 pm 
 Last modified: 31 October, 2026, 05:42 pm 
 Still from the Korean webtoon, Tower of God. Photo: Collected "> 
 Still from the Korean webtoon, Tower of God. Photo: Collected 
 At the swipe of a thumb, a new cultural wave is taking hold among Bangladesh's urban youth. What started as pandemic-era screen escapism has evolved into a growing fascination with South Korean webtoons – or manhwa . Beyond the screen, their influence is spilling into fashion, conversations, and everyday social life, quietly weaving another thread of Hallyu into Bangladesh's youth culture. 
 For some young Bangladeshis, a Korean webtoon is more than something to read before bed. It can lead them to a drama, a song, a fashion trend, a new friendship – or simply make them curious about a culture that once felt very far away.
 It often starts innocently. Someone sends a link.
 Keep updated, follow The Business Standard's Google news channel
 "Read this. You'll love it."
 You open it on your phone, read one episode, and tell yourself you will stop there. You don't.
 One episode becomes five. Five becomes 20. Soon, you end up waiting for the next update, searching for fan theories and looking up the meaning of a Korean word that appeared in the story.
 And somewhere along the way, the webtoon becomes more than a story.
 For a growing number of young people around the world, South Korean webtoons have become one of the many ways they encounter Korean culture. Bangladesh is no exception.
 The Korean Wave, or Hallyu, is already familiar to Bangladeshi youth. K-pop, K-dramas, films, and animated shows and anime, Korean food, skincare, and fashion have all found their way into everyday conversations and social media feeds. The Korean Embassy in Dhaka regularly highlights their growing popularity among young Bangladeshis.
 But the part of the Korean Wave that still gets less attention is webtoons.
 However, because they were created for the digital age, webtoons fit particularly well into the way young Bangladeshis already consume culture – through a phone, a screen, and a constant stream of recommendations from friends and social media.
 It starts with a story 
 Unlike the comics many of us grew up reading in printed form, webtoons are made to be scrolled.
 The format is simple. Open your phone, scroll down, and keep reading.
 But the experience can be surprisingly immersive.
 The stories range from romance and comedy to fantasy, thriller, action, and drama. Some follow ordinary school or workplace relationships. Others take readers into completely fictional worlds.
 A still from the Korean webtoon Solo Leveling. Photo: Collected "> 
 A still from the Korean webtoon Solo Leveling. Photo: Collected 
 What makes them particularly powerful is that the characters are not just characters. Readers notice what they wear, how they speak, where they live, and what they eat. They become attached to their personalities and relationships, and that can make a distant culture feel a little less distant.
 A reader who has never visited South Korea may become familiar with Korean names, food, school life, social expressions, and even small everyday habits simply by following a fictional character's life.
 That curiosity can then travel elsewhere.
 A webtoon can lead to a drama adaptation. The drama can lead to K-pop. A song can lead to a Korean-language video. A social-media post can lead to a fashion trend. The journey does not have a fixed starting point.
 Hallyu doesn't come in one package 
 This is what makes webtoons interesting in Bangladesh's Hallyu story.
 Korean culture does not reach young people through one single medium anymore.
 A person might discover South Korea through BTS or BLACKPINK. Someone else might start with " Crash Landing on You" or " True Beauty" . Another might first encounter Korea through skincare or food.
 And then there are readers who enter through webtoons.
 Sometimes the journey goes in the opposite direction.
 A K-drama fan discovers that the series they just watched was based on a webtoon. They find the original story and start reading it. Then they discover another webtoon by the same creator.
 Suddenly, one form of Korean entertainment has opened the door to another.
 That interconnectedness is at the heart of modern Hallyu.
 Research on Korean popular culture in Bangladesh has already shown how digital platforms and fan communities help young people consume Korean culture and connect with one another around it.
 Webtoons simply add another route into that network.
 When a fictional character influences real life 
 The influence does not necessarily stop when the reader closes the app.
 Scroll through social media and you can see how easily fictional worlds spill into real ones.
 A character's oversized sweater gets recreated in an outfit post. A hairstyle becomes a reference for a haircut. A reader searches for a Korean brand worn by a character.
 This does not mean every person who reads a webtoon suddenly starts dressing like a Korean character.
 Cultural influence rarely works that neatly. Instead, young people tend to pick and choose. 
 A Korean-inspired outfit might be combined with clothes they already wear. A Korean aesthetic might be adapted to Bangladesh's weather, culture and budget. A phrase picked up from a webtoon might appear alongside Bangla and English in a social-media caption.
 In other words, they are not simply copying Korean culture.
 They are making something of their own from it.
 This is also visible in Bangladesh's wider relationship with Korean fashion. K-pop and K-dramas have already influenced the way some young Bangladeshis experiment with oversized clothing, minimalist styling, colours, accessories, and Korean-inspired looks. 
 Still from the Korean Webtoon, True Beauty. Photo: Collected "> 
 Still from the Korean Webtoon, True Beauty. Photo: Collected 
 Webtoons can become another visual source of inspiration, especially because fashion is such an important part of their storytelling.
 A story becomes a social activity 
 Something else also happens when people read the same webtoon.
 They talk about it.
 A friend recommends a series. Someone posts a favourite character on Facebook. Another person shares a theory about what will happen in the next chapter.
 Someone else says, "You have to read this one."
 And suddenly, reading is no longer a completely solitary activity.
 This is one of the defining features of fandom culture today.
 Bangladesh already has active communities built around Korean popular culture. Groups and fan communities have created spaces where young people can meet others who share their interests, attend events, and participate in Korean-themed activities.
 Webtoon readers are finding themselves part of a much wider community, as their interest grows, so does the urge to share it with others. Dedicated social media groups and online communities focused solely on manhwa are slowly emerging, giving Bangladeshi readers a space to discuss favourite stories, exchange recommendations, and connect over a shared fascination.
 That may be one of the biggest differences between today's Hallyu and the Korean cultural influence of the past.
 Young audiences are not just watching. They are commenting, sharing, creating, recommending, and meeting. They are participating.
 From Korea to Bangladesh — and back again 
 Perhaps the most interesting part is what happens when Korean culture reaches Bangladesh and is changed in the process.
 A webtoon written in South Korea is read by someone in Dhaka. The reader interprets the story through their own experiences. They discuss it with Bangladeshi friends. They may explain Korean expressions to someone else. They may mix Korean references with Bangla humour.
 The original culture remains Korean. But the way it is experienced is distinctly local.
 That is why it may be misleading to think of Hallyu as a one-way flow from South Korea to the rest of the world. Digital platforms have made that relationship much more complicated.
 Korean creators produce the content. Platforms distribute it. Bangladeshi audiences consume it. Fans discuss and reinterpret it. Social media carries those interpretations further.
 The audience becomes part of the cultural journey.
 The next chapter of Hallyu? 
 For years, conversations about South Korean culture in Bangladesh have largely focused on K-pop and K-dramas.
 Webtoons suggest that the story may be getting bigger.
 They sit at an interesting intersection between entertainment, technology, and everyday culture. They can be read anywhere, shared instantly, and connected to other forms of Korean entertainment.
 Most importantly, they can become personal.
 A reader may remember a character who helped them through a difficult week. Another may discover a new interest because of a story. Someone may make friends through a shared fandom. Someone else may simply find a new style of clothing they like.
 None of these experiences, on their own, prove that webtoons are transforming Bangladeshi society.
 But together, they raise an interesting question.
 What happens when a story created thousands of kilometres away becomes part of someone's ordinary life here?
 Perhaps that is where the newer story of Hallyu lies — not simply in how successfully Korean culture travels to Bangladesh, but in what Bangladeshi young people do with it once it arrives.
 A webtoon may begin with a swipe.
 But the cultural journey can go much further.
